From Saturn's magnificent rings to the waning gibbous moon, here's how to turn your Thanksgiving celebrations into a family skywatching adventure.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

If your household is like most American families, then on Thursday you likely will all be sitting down with family and friends for a traditional Thanksgiving turkey dinner during the mid-to-late afternoon hours.

Then as darkness falls, some will probably migrate into the living room to catch some football or other holiday fare on television. But if you have a large gathering of family and friends at your home — and if your skies are mainly clear — why not invite everyone outside to gaze at the evening sky?

If you have binoculars, or better yet, a telescope, you just might end up turning this into a memorable family tradition of its own.

If I may paraphrase the mysterious voice from the 1989 movie, "Field of Dreams": "If you set up your telescope, they will come." And you'll get a big kick out of your Turkey Day guests uttering all the "oohs" and "ahs" or exclamations of "Wow!" with just one peek through the eyepiece.

As darkness falls, Saturn will glow at first magnitude, shining with a sedate, yellow-white light and appearing noticeably brighter than the star Fomalhaut, about 40 degrees (the equivalent of four fist-widths) to its lower right.

Its famous ring system is now tilted only about six degrees toward Earth but may be visible with steadied (or image-stabilized) high-power binoculars or through the eyepiece of a telescope magnifying over 30-power. The rings will seem to glow with an inner light and for those who have never had the pleasure of seeing them for themselves, that first view always elicits astonishment; kids especially most often will say: "Awesome!" or "No way!" I've even had people accuse me of using a slide of Saturn, to which I, of course, reply with, "No . . . that's the real thing."

Then, along about 6:25 p.m. local time, the waning gibbous moon, 2½ days past full phase and 91% illuminated, will begin to emerge from beyond the east-northeast horizon. Give it another hour and it will stand about 10 degrees above the horizon — equal to the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length. By then, the moon will be in a better position for evening study.

Even in binoculars, the moon is a striking sight to see. It's such a special object because it doesn't matter whether you live in a rural area or in the middle of a brightly lit city, for the moon can always be readily observed. It always looks spectacular whether you're using binoculars or a telescope. It never looks precisely the same no matter how often you view it and can be observed even on hazy or partially cloud-covered nights.

Pay particular attention to the line of darkness — called the terminator — features near that border stand out in bold relief; the shadows become stronger and details are more easily seen. Take note on this night of the circular dark area, bisected by the terminator: Mare Crisium — the "Sea of Crises." Immediately bordering above it is a 50-mile (80 km)-wide ring of very rugged mountains, rising as high as 14,400 feet (4,389 meters), which now resembles a huge crater partially in shadow when the sun is low.

Probably the one object that your Thanksgiving guests will want to see is the biggest and brightest of all the man-made objects orbiting the Earth: the International Space Station (ISS). Except for those living across the southern US, for most everywhere else, the ISS will be making visible passes on Thanksgiving evening.

Circling the Earth at an average altitude of 260 miles (420 km) and at a speed of 17,500 mph (28,200 kph), it can appear to move as fast as a high-flying jet airliner, sometimes taking as much as six or seven minutes to cross the sky. It can easily be confused with aircraft lights. Nominally, it appears white with a slight yellow tinge and at its very brightest it can sometimes appear to shine as bright as magnitude -5.6, which is twice as bright as the planet Venus! So, what is the viewing schedule on Thanksgiving for your hometown? You can easily find out by visiting one of three popular websites:

This site will tell you when and where to sight the ISS. All you need do is type in your city or town, then click on the map pinpoint to get all the details. You can even sign up to get email or text alerts when the space station is flying over.

This site will not only provide you with sighting information for the ISS, but also for many other satellites as well. You must first register and then you can input your location to generate a sighting schedule.

Like Heavens Above, you can get sighting information for the ISS and other satellites. Once you log on this site will automatically provide details based on your IP address ... or you can set a "custom" location.

Here at Space.com, we like to wish a very happy and safe Thanksgiving to all, and of course, clear skies!

#572. Has AI just cracked Internet encryption? Rumoured ‘bombshell’ stuns scientists

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from online banking and private messages to sensitive government communications.Credit: Peshkov/Getty

Artificial-intelligence agents have already begun to wreak havoc by hacking into servers around the world, either spontaneously or directed by humans. Now, a threat is emerging that is on a whole other scale.

Several computer scientists have suggested on social media that the leading AI laboratories — companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, both in San Francisco, California — have discovered algorithms that could derail the security of Internet communications.

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

‘If we can solve Riemann, what can’t we do?’: mathematicians shocked and excited by AI breakthroughs

“I’m virtually certain, from multiple reliable sources, that the AI labs are now sitting on one or more bombshells,” computer scientist Scott Aaronson wrote yesterday on his blog. The details are still hazy, added Aaronson, who is at the University of Texas at Austin. “Until I either see details or hear directly from someone at a lab, I feel much, much less confident about the specific nature of those bombshells.”

The algorithms are rumoured to target the information-scrambling system known as RSA, which relies on the mathematics of prime numbers, as well as more-advanced technologies.

While the rumours could not be confirmed, other breakthroughs announced by the AI companies this week make researchers cautiously optimistic that the mathematics of encryption could eventually come to help.

Nature examines the threat, and what can be done about it.

Several researchers say they have heard that some of the leading AI laboratories have discovered algorithms capable of breaking public-key cryptography in ‘polynomial time’ (or ‘P’ in computer-science shorthand).

Public-key cryptography helps to secure everything from banking apps to Internet browsers. It relies on mathematical problems that are considered practically impossible for computers to solve within a reasonable amount of time.

An algorithm that could solve these problems in polynomial time would change that. It means the time needed to solve a problem would increase relatively slowly as the problem gets larger. For example, a password of length n could be broken in a number of steps proportional to the square or cube of its size (n² or n³).

The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers

The race to save the Internet from quantum hackers

Theoretical computer scientists tend to think of P problems as relatively easy to solve, especially compared with problems that require exponential time, where the number of steps might grow as 2n, for example. As n gets larger — or a password gets longer — the time required by an exponential algorithm quickly exceeds that of any polynomial one.

In practical terms, an algorithm that could break public-key cryptography in polynomial time could undermine much of the security on which the Internet relies.

It depends on which encryption systems they could crack, and how efficiently they could do so.

One of the most ubiquitous techniques for establishing public keys is to multiply two large prime numbers. This technique, called RSA, was long believed to be secure because ‘cracking the code’ requires factoring that product back into the original primes, a much slower process (at least, without a powerful quantum computer, which does not yet exist). One of the rumours now circulating is that the AI labs have found an algorithm that can do this.

But even though a polynomial-time algorithm could be very powerful on paper, it could still be impossible to use except for the shortest passwords. An algorithm requiring n10000steps, for example, be very impractical to apply.

However, proving that a problem is in ‘P’, even if the polynomial-time solution is practically useless, has usually been followed by improvements that have eventually led to efficient solutions. “The issue is that the idea that [the problem] was hard — because of needing exponential time — is dead,” Aaronson tells Nature.

Not necessarily. This type of worst-case scenario hinges on a long-standing open question known as ‘P = NP’: could every problem whose solution can be checked in polynomial time also be solved in polynomial time? If so, problems that underpin essentially all public-key cryptography could become much easier to crack.

Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security

Quantum-computing pioneer warns of complacency over Internet security

But most researchers think that this is unlikely. In fact, some recent AI-aided results have made them cautiously optimistic. Earlier this week, both Anthropic and OpenAI announced results in theoretical computer science that suggest that many similar problems could be hard to solve. Before the recent explosion in AI-aided maths, each of those advances would have been hailed as the computer-science breakthrough of the decade, Aaronson says.

Ryan Williams, a computer scientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in Cambridge, agrees. “I am definitely blown away by the latest developments.” One especially interesting result, he says, shows that for a ubiquitous type of computation called matrix multiplication, the exponent in a polynomial-time algorithm cannot be too small. “Underneath the hood, it seems to provide a brand-new framework for proving limitations on efficient computation,” says Williams.

#571. Physicists just sent an unblockable message through a brick wall using gravity

Researchers at the University of Queensland have demonstrated an unusual new way to communicate, using gravity to send a message directly through a brick wall. Instead of relying on radio waves or other electromagnetic signals, the team used an old elevator, a massive counterweight, and an extremely sensitive instrument capable of detecting tiny changes in gravitational pull.

The experiment took place inside UQ's Parnell Building. Physicists repeatedly moved an elevator between two floors, shifting its 1.8-metric-ton counterweight between two positions. Each position represented a binary digit, either 0 or 1, allowing the researchers to encode information through the movement of the heavy mass.

On the other side of a brick wall, a device called a gravimeter was positioned in a nearby bathroom. The instrument measured the extremely small changes in gravity produced by the moving counterweight. By decoding those measurements, the team successfully recovered a one-word message: 'Gravity'.

Why Gravity Could Succeed Where Wi-Fi Fails

The experiment highlights a potentially important advantage of using gravity for communication. Unlike conventional wireless signals, which can be weakened or blocked by physical obstacles, gravitational fields pass through ordinary materials without being screened out.

Dr. Charles Woffinden from UQ's School of Mathematics and Physics explained why this property makes gravity an intriguing alternative to existing communication technologies.

"Unlike the electromagnetic signals used in modern wireless communication, a gravitational signal cannot simply be screened out by placing ordinary material in its path," Dr. Woffinden said.

"Anyone who has lost phone reception in a tunnel or struggled with Wi-Fi through a solid wall will understand the appeal.

"While the present system is far from practical, it demonstrates the possibility of communicating using a method that ordinary physical barriers cannot block."

The basic principle is surprisingly simple. Any object with mass produces a gravitational field, and moving that object changes the field around it. Although these changes are generally far too small for people to notice, sufficiently sensitive instruments can detect them. By controlling how a large mass moves, researchers can create a sequence of gravitational changes that represents digital information.

The idea for the experiment emerged from a separate research effort that had little to do with communication.

Dr. Andrew Groszek said the team had originally been developing a contactless weighbridge, a system designed to measure the weight of vehicles without requiring them to drive onto a conventional scale.

"We were aiming to determine the mass of trucks and other large vehicles by measuring their tiny gravitational pull," Dr. Groszek said.

"Once we had shown that the idea worked, we realized the same physics could be used to encode and transmit information."

That realization opened the door to a different application. If a sensitive detector could measure the gravitational influence of a large vehicle, it could also detect deliberately controlled changes in the position of a heavy object. Those changes could then be used to represent the ones and zeros that form the foundation of digital communication.

Despite its success, the demonstration revealed a major obstacle to practical gravity-based communication: transmitting information this way is extraordinarily slow.

Professor Andrew White explained that the elevator's age and limited speed placed a severe restriction on how quickly the researchers could send their message.

"Our lift was snail-paced - it's from the 1950s - so our experiment transmitted just 1 bit per minute, meaning it took an hour to send a single word," Professor White said.

For comparison, a bit is the smallest unit of digital information, representing either a 0 or a 1. Modern communication systems transmit enormous numbers of bits every second. The gravity experiment, by contrast, required an entire minute to communicate just one bit.

According to White, improving the system would require finding ways to produce detectable gravitational changes more quickly.

"The speed of gravity communication would come down to how big the mass is, how fast you can move it, and the sensitivity of the detector.

"It took more than 100 years to go from the first telegraph system to the mobile phone, so while gravity communication is not practical today, it could be in the future."

Could Quantum Sensors Make Gravity Communication Practical?

Although the experiment relied on a conventional gravity sensor, the researchers believe more advanced technology could eventually make the approach faster and capable of operating over greater distances.

Professor Matthew Davis emphasized that the team's most important achievement was demonstrating that gravity could be used to transmit recoverable information.

"It's not often that you get to demonstrate an entirely new way of communicating," Professor Davis said.

"We have shown experimentally that information can be encoded in the gravitational field and recovered at the other end.

"Our experiment used a classical gravity sensor, but our modeling indicates that quantum sensors could, with rather ambitious assumptions, support ranges of up to about 500 meters and data rates of around 15 bits per minute."

Quantum sensors exploit properties of quantum physics to make exceptionally precise measurements. In principle, their greater sensitivity could allow researchers to detect much smaller gravitational changes, potentially improving both the range and speed of gravity-based communication.

However, the team's projections depend on ambitious assumptions, and the suggested performance has not yet been demonstrated experimentally. Even at 15 bits per minute, the system would remain dramatically slower than modern wireless technologies.

Still, the potential applications are intriguing. A sufficiently advanced gravity-based communication system could someday transmit information in environments where radio waves, light, and other conventional signals cannot penetrate.

For now, an aging elevator and a gravimeter in a university bathroom have demonstrated something remarkable: information can be carried by changes in gravity and recovered on the other side of a solid wall.

The research was published in Science Advances.

Luca Guadagnino wants to return to romance.

Speaking to Variety at the Marrakech Film Festival where he’s presenting “Artificial,” the Italian filmmaker behind “Call Me by Your Name,” “Bones and All” and “Queer” revealed that he hopes his next directorial endeavor will be another love story.

“I think a lot of inspiration could come from facts of history,” Guadagnino said when asked what he would like to explore in his next film. “I want to make another love story, so I have to think about it, but I want to make a kind movie, another love story.” Related Stories Documentaries at the Oscars: A History of Breaking Out of Their Category — and What It Means for ‘You Can See Everything’ Oscars: Best Original Score — Could One of Hollywood’s Most Overlooked Composers Finally Get His Moment?

“I want to make another love story, a kind movie,” Luca Guadagnino said at #MarrakechFilmFestival.However, the Italian director confirmed that the queer romance “Separate Rooms,” originally set to star Josh O’Connor, is no longer in the works. Guadagnino also addressed the… pic.twitter.com/kTmz3PlAZr

He also confirmed that two of his previously announced projects — a new adaptation of Bret Easton Ellis’ “American Psycho” and the gay romance “Separate Rooms” — are no longer moving forward with him.

“Separate Rooms” was set to be an adaptation of Italian writer Pier Vittorio Tondelli’s 1989 novel about a writer grappling with the death of his lover. Josh O’Connor, who previously worked with Guadagnino on “Challengers,” and Léa Seydoux had been linked to the project since 2024.

“I don’t think I’m doing a movie with Léa Seydoux, unfortunately. That’s not happening,” Guadagnino said. “But I would love to work with Léa, of course.”

The director also addressed the demise of his “American Psycho” adaptation, which was first announced by Lionsgate in October 2024. The film, penned by Scott Z. Burns, was intended to be a fresh interpretation of Ellis’ 1991 novel rather than a remake of Mary Harron’s 2000 cult classic starring Christian Bale. “That’s the job of a director,” he said of its dissolution. “You direct movies and sometimes it happens, sometimes it doesn’t. It’s very simple and linear and usual.”

The filmmaker also dispelled speculation that Robert Pattinson had been in contention to play Patrick Bateman, though he said “he’s a perfect choice for James Bond,” adding: “He’s an incredible star, he’s done so many great roles and I wish someday to work with him, of course.”

Would Guadagnino direct a Bond film? “I would say yes, yes, of course,” he said of the prospect. “I would like to play with icons.”

The director’s upcoming film, “Artificial,” marks another departure from the sweeping romances that have come to define much of his oeuvre. The Amazon MGM Studios feature dramatizes the turmoil at OpenAI surrounding the ousting and subsequent reinstatement of CEO Sam Altman, played by Andrew Garfield.

The film premiered at New York Film Festival and screens at Marrakech Film Festival on Thursday night.

#568. Iran balances ties with China and Russia as Trump ramps up pressure

As Donald Trump seeks to tighten economic pressure on Iran, China remains its biggest oil customer and Russia a key partner. But both powers are balancing support for Tehran against broader interests with Washington.

As Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin meet in Shenzhen, Washington wants to tighten its blockade of Iran, but China remains Tehran's main oil buyer and Russia offers it political and logistical support.

For Iran, relations with both China and Russia are routinely described as strategic. That relationship looks more complicated from Beijing and Moscow.

Both countries oppose Washington's efforts to isolate Iran and maintain political and economic ties with Tehran. But both have broader interests in their relationships with the United States and may see Iran partly through the prism of their own negotiations with Washington.

That raises a central question: Can Trump's strategy of economically isolating Iran succeed if China and Russia refuse to fully cooperate?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

China is currently the most important destination for Iranian oil.

In 2025, it was reported that Chinese buyers took more than 80% of Iran's seaborne crude exports, much of it through independent refiners and at a steep discount because of sanctions.

As China provided Tehran an economic lifeline, Iran also became increasingly dependent on Chinese manufactured goods, machinery and industrial inputs.

Mohsen Solhdoost, an assistant professor of international relations at Xi'an Jiaotong-Liverpool University, says China is important to Washington's strategy but not decisive on its own.

"If the objective is to reduce Iranian export earnings, restrict access to equipment and make economic and military recovery more difficult, the United States can achieve substantial results without Chinese cooperation," he told DW.

But forcing Iran to accept Washington's preferred nuclear or regional policies is another matter.

"The ability to interrupt trade is much easier to demonstrate than the ability to determine another government's political choices," Solhdoost said.

That distinction has become more important as US sanctions enforcement and maritime blockade efforts have increased pressure on Iranian crude oil exports.

In November, Washington announced Task Force Iron Gate, an initiative aimed at disrupting the movement of sanctioned goods, military equipment and revenue through Iran's land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Even so, these trade links have not disappeared. The commercial and security interests of countries including Iraq, Pakistan and Turkey mean that goods continue to move across the region, albeit under greater scrutiny.

As a result, China's role in Iran's economy remains significant, but Solhdoost argues that demand alone cannot sustain Iranian exports. The oil must be able to reach international markets.

"A Chinese buyer cannot keep Iranian export revenues flowing simply by remaining willing to buy if newly loaded tankers cannot reach the market," Solhdoost said.

This economic pressure is shaping Tehran's financial planning. A senior official at Iran's Plan and Budget Organization recently said the government was preparing its 2027-2028 budget under several scenarios, including one in which oil revenue falls to zero.

That does not mean Iran has adopted a zero-oil budget, but considering such a scenario illustrates how seriously Tehran views the situation. At the same time, Chinese trade can preserve critical parts of the Iranian economy even if overall commerce shrinks.

Machinery, electronics, spare parts and industrial components can still reach Iran by rail and road. Such trade cannot replace maritime commerce at comparable scale or cost, but it can keep selected factories and infrastructure operating.

Such Chinese support could help Iran endure pressure without preventing economic deterioration, says Solhdoost.

But even for Beijing, supporting Iran economically does not mean supporting every Iranian policy.

Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi has maintained support for cooperation with Tehran while calling for negotiations, safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz and stable energy supplies.

A prolonged conflict around Hormuz threatens wider energy supplies and global shipping. China therefore benefits from continued access to Iranian oil but also from regional stability.

Russia creates another obstacle to Iran's isolation. The two countries share access to the Caspian Sea and have expanded military, transport and economic cooperation.

Iranian officials have discussed ways of using Russian and northern trade routes to reduce the impact of American restrictions. There has also been speculation about oil swaps and deeper Russian assistance, although these claims remain difficult to verify.

Ahmad Vakhshiteh, director of the Moscow-based Center for Strategic Research on Developing Relations with the Middle East, believes the summit should be viewed within a larger attempt to manage the wars in both Ukraine and the Middle East.

"Russia, China and the United States appear to be seeking constructive dialogue and results that could shape a new security architecture in the international system," Vakhshiteh told DW.

Solhdoost also warns against overstating Russian support for Iran.

The strategic partnership between Moscow and Tehran provides for security cooperation and efforts to counter unilateral sanctions, but it does not require Russia to enter a war on Iran's behalf.

Since Russia is deeply engaged in Ukraine, it likely has its own priorities in negotiations with Washington, says Solhdoost.

"Russia would prioritize its own national interests in negotiations with the US over Ukraine and Iran," he said.

Moscow could support Iran while simultaneously using its relationship with Tehran as leverage in talks with Trump over Ukraine.

For Iran, ties with China and Russia remain essential. They provide alternative trade routes, export markets and diplomatic support that complicate Washington's efforts to isolate Tehran.

Yet neither Beijing nor Moscow views Iran solely through the lens of strategic partnership. Both weigh support for Tehran against their own economic interests, security concerns and dealings with Washington.

#567. Earth's next ice age may have already begun. Global warming stopped it

About 2,000 years ago, the remnants of a massive ice sheet in the Canadian Arctic began expanding once again. According to new research, this slow buildup of ice may have marked the beginning of Earth's next glacial period, commonly called an ice age. But something unexpected happened. By the 1960s, rising summer temperatures had reversed the trend, causing the ice to retreat instead of grow.

The findings suggest that global warming may have interrupted a new ice age that was already getting underway, fundamentally altering a natural climate cycle that has shaped Earth for millions of years.

"It was just getting started, everything was normal, the next glaciation was about to happen -- and yet it stopped," says Nicolás Young, a geochemist at Columbia Climate School's Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. "It's a very powerful example of how we have jolted the system."

Ancient Arctic Ice Reveals a Surprising Climate History

In a study published in Science, Young and fellow Lamont geochemist Joerg Schaefer, along with their colleagues, investigated the history of the Laurentide Ice Sheet. This enormous mass of ice covered much of Canada and the northern United States between approximately 95,000 and 20,000 years ago.

At its greatest extent, the Laurentide stretched from north of the Arctic Circle all the way south to Illinois. In some locations, its ice was more than two miles thick. Although most of this enormous ice sheet disappeared as the climate warmed, one surviving piece remains.

Known as the Barnes Ice Cap, this ancient remnant sits on central Baffin Island in Nunavut, Canada, and covers an area roughly the size of Delaware.

"People always say that it disappeared, but that's not true," says Young.

Scientists already knew that the Laurentide Ice Sheet had repeatedly grown and retreated during the roughly 2.6 million years since extensive continental glaciation began in North America. What remained uncertain was whether the ice sheet had ever become smaller than it is today before expanding again.

Answering that question could reveal whether a new cycle of glaciation had begun much more recently than scientists previously believed.

(A note on terminology: Technically, we are still living in an ice age-the Late Cenozoic Ice Age-which started about 34 million years ago. Within it, colder glacial periods alternate with warmer interglacial ones, including the one we live in now. What people casually call an "ice age" is usually a glacial period. The last glacial period ended about 11,700 years ago.)

Ancient Plants Preserved Beneath Ice Hold the Clues

Piecing together the history of an ice sheet is particularly challenging when researchers are looking for evidence of its smallest extent and earliest stages of regrowth. As glaciers advance, they frequently scrape across the land, destroying the geological traces that could reveal where and when the ice first began spreading.

The Barnes Ice Cap, however, offers an unusual opportunity to investigate this history.

Unlike most glaciers, it is frozen directly to the bedrock beneath it and does not slide across the landscape. As a result, plants that once grew in areas later covered by expanding ice can remain preserved in place for thousands of years.

Since the Barnes Ice Cap began retreating in 1960, previously buried vegetation has gradually emerged from beneath the melting ice. Researchers can collect these ancient plant remains and determine when they were alive using radiocarbon dating.

This technique measures carbon-14, a harmlessly radioactive form of carbon that living organisms absorb from the atmosphere. Once an organism dies, its carbon-14 begins breaking down at a predictable rate. By measuring how much remains, scientists can estimate when the plant stopped growing and became buried beneath the ice.

These dates provide a record of when the advancing glacier covered different parts of the landscape.

"If you do this enough times, you can actually develop a timeline of that ice margin systematically advancing over plants. You're actually tracking the expansion of that ice margin," says Young.

Earth's Next Ice Age May Have Begun 2,000 Years Ago

The research team examined ancient vegetation uncovered by the retreating Barnes Ice Cap, along with plant remains exposed beneath smaller ice caps that have recently melted in the surrounding region.

Together, these samples allowed the scientists to reconstruct thousands of years of glacial change.

Their results indicate that the Laurentide Ice Sheet reached its smallest extent approximately 3,000 years ago. Then, around 2,000 years ago, temperatures became cold enough for the remaining ice to begin expanding again.

Young and his colleagues argue that this renewed growth should be recognized as the start of Earth's next glacial period.

That interpretation differs from previous research based on climate models, which has generally suggested that the next glaciation would not begin for thousands or even tens of thousands of years.

The disagreement partly comes down to how scientists define the beginning of a glacial period. Rather than waiting until enormous ice sheets have spread across continents, Young's team proposes that the first sustained expansion of an existing ice sheet should mark the starting point.

Under that definition, the next glaciation had already begun long before modern scientists recognized it.

The discovery also casts new light on a controversial scientific debate from the 1970s, when some climate researchers suggested that another ice age might be approaching.

"It actually was happening," Young says. "They couldn't quite prove it, but now we sort of have the evidence."

However, this early expansion would not have produced an immediate or dramatic transformation of the planet. According to Young, it would have taken thousands of years for the cooling to become noticeable and roughly 30,000 years for the Laurentide Ice Sheet to regain its enormous continental dimensions.

The process was only in its earliest stages when the warming climate brought it to a halt.

Global Warming Reversed the Growth of the Ice Sheet

By the 1960s, conditions had changed enough that the Barnes Ice Cap was losing more ice during the summer than it could replace through winter snowfall.

Instead of continuing to expand, the ancient ice began shrinking.

According to the researchers' interpretation, this reversal effectively ended the developing glacial period before it could progress into a full-scale ice age.

The consequences may extend far beyond the present day. Models projecting the future of the Barnes Ice Cap indicate that it could disappear entirely within the next few centuries.

"That will be the true very last remains of the Laurentide, disappearing for good," Young says.

The Loss of an Ancient Ice Cap Could Change Future Ice Ages

The disappearance of the Barnes Ice Cap could also have implications for how future glacial periods develop.

In the past, the Laurentide Ice Sheet provided a starting point for renewed glaciation whenever Earth's climate cooled sufficiently. Because a large existing mass of ice helps create conditions favorable for further ice accumulation, it can trigger reinforcing processes that allow glaciers to expand.

Scientists describe this kind of process as a positive feedback. In this case, existing ice helps promote the growth of additional ice, allowing an ice sheet to become increasingly extensive as temperatures remain cold.

Without the Laurentide's last surviving remnant, a future glacial period might unfold differently.

Researchers cannot yet determine when another glaciation could begin under atmospheric conditions influenced by elevated greenhouse gas concentrations. If enormous continental ice sheets eventually start forming again, they may have to develop without the ancient ice that previously helped initiate their growth.

The findings suggest that global warming has done more than melt glaciers and shrink existing ice sheets. It may have interrupted a glacial cycle that was already beginning, while also removing a feature that helped sustain ice age cycles across North America for millions of years.

"What has been an extremely natural and predictable phenomenon is now gone," says Young.

#566. Chiwetel Ejiofor on How Stephen Frears’ ‘Dirty Pretty Things’ Led Him to Fall in Love With Film

Chiwetel Ejiofor started his film career by doing something that many would consider as the absolute peak: he made a film with Steven Spielberg.

“Amistad” was his very first film and, understandably, he was afraid of peaking too soon.

“I was definitely worried about it at the time,” he said at Torino Film Festival. Related Stories Oscar Predictions: Costume Design — Will the Academy Embrace the Three Distinct Eras of ‘La Bola Negra’? ‘Michael’ Won’t Be Submitted for BAFTA Awards as Filmmakers Pass on Billion-Dollar Biopic’s Entry (EXCLUSIVE)

“You feel that there are stages to how you develop as an actor and the opportunities you get, and you think they might follow a very linear path. But of course, my first film role was with Steven Spielberg. I realized then, very early on, that it’s a deeply unpredictable profession. You can either feel disquiet or anxiety about that, or you have to go with it.”

He added: “The opportunities can be sporadic or come from different places and angles that you didn’t imagine. Part of the challenge, but also the exciting thing about being an actor, is having the capacity and ability to roll with it, to travel on the journey of it and see where it takes you.”

The British actor came to Italy to receive the Stella della Mole award for lifetime achievement.

He admitted that, for the longest time, he didn’t see himself as a film actor.

“Even though I had done the Steven Spielberg film, I still thought of myself primarily as a theater actor. I worked with the National Theatre in Great Britain, in the West End and with many off-West End theater companies,” he said. In 2008, he won the Laurence Olivier Award for best actor for “Othello.”

It took Stephen Frears’ thriller “Dirty Pretty Things” – which screened at Torino Film Festival on Thursday – to finally change his mind. Frears also received an award at the festival this week.

“I think it was around that time when I started to fall in love with film as well, with film acting and the rhythm and poetry of cinema. A lot of that had to do with Stephen Frears and Chris Menges, who was the cinematographer on that film. It became something that I started to pursue.”

For a while, he was able to “balance the two very well.”

“It was when I became more involved in writing and directing that it started taking up a lot of my time outside of acting in films. Historically, this would have been the time I spent on stage. I ended up writing or directing my own films.”

Ejiofor has directed two feature films: “Rob Peace” and “The Boy Who Harnessed the Wind.” But his return to theater is imminent.

“It’s still something that I’m very passionate about. Finding the time to do as much theater as I want can be challenging, but it’s something I’m in the midst of conversations about.”

He hopes to be involved in another theater production later on next year. In the meantime, he’s happy to reflect on some of the highlights of his career, which includes Oscar-winning “12 Years a Slave,” directed by Steve McQueen, also shown at the Italian fest.

In the film, he played Solomon Northup, a free black man who was kidnapped in 1841 and sold into slavery in Louisiana.

“I hadn’t heard of his story at all. When I was sent the script, I was incredibly moved and shocked by it. Then I read Northup’s own memoir. I thought it was an extraordinary story, an extraordinary tale,” he said before the screening, praising the story that captured a “very tragic period of absence of humanity.”

“It felt very profound to me. I was just deeply moved. Steve McQueen is a phenomenal filmmaker, incredibly passionate, detailed and thorough, with a wonderful vision and cinematic heart. It was incredibly gratifying to see the film being received the way that it was, globally and by the Academy.”

He noted: “At its heart, it was always a story about human respect and human dignity.”

The striking blue of the Betta Fish Nebula swims across the cosmic landscape, a stunning wisp of material leftover from a stellar explosion.

Roughly 6,800 light-years from Earth and nestled in the Centaurus constellation, this piece of the supernova remnant SNR G295.5+09.7 has earned the nickname the Betta Fish Nebula for its floaty, fishy shape.

This almost ghostly whirl of gas and dust was created when a star much more massive than our sun exploded, blasting its outer layers of material outward in the process. Over time, the remnants of this supernova eruption stretched outward into space, dispersing and colliding with surrounding gas. The explosive remnants mixing with gas in the interstellar medium created this glowing, blue cloud.

This celestial scene was captured by the Dark Energy Camera (DECam), that was created by the U.S. Department of Energy. The camera is installed on the National Science Foundation's Víctor M. Blanco 4-meter Telescope in Chile.

This image of a colossal, cosmic "fish" was captured by a camera meant to study the illusive effects of dark energy, which is the name scientists have given for whatever mysterious something is causing the universe to expand at an accelerating rate.

The camera is used as part of the Dark Energy Survey, a six-year, international collaboration in which scientists have collected observations of hundreds of millions of galaxies, thousands of supernova and additional details about our cosmos that could help to fill in the picture of the nature of dark energy.

And while researchers this past January revealed the initial result of this six-year survey, scientists continue to explore the possibilities of dark energy with DECam alongside instruments like the recently-launched Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope.

However, while the survey has lofty goals with its DECam data, the camera can also capture beautiful imagery like this cerulean wisp thousands of light-years away.

#564. Wadephul: 'Coalition of the Willing' talks in Berlin send strong signal to Moscow

German Foreign Minister Wadephul has said the Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin sends a clear message to Moscow to take peace talks seriously. He also warned Ukraine should be prepared for peace talks to fail.

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul said Thursday's meeting of the "Coalition of the Willing" in Berlin sent a strong signal to Moscow that it was time to take negotiations to end the war in Ukraine seriously.

Speaking to DW during a visit to the South Caucasus, Wadephul described the summit as the largest meeting of Ukraine's supporters so far. The meeting represents the 18th set of high-level talks among the coalition's members.

He said it demonstrated that allies remained firmly behind Kyiv in the fifth year of Russia's war and were ready to do "what was necessary to ensure Ukraine could negotiate from a position of strength."

"The summit itself is already a success," he told DW.

Wadephul also welcomed the US initiative to restart peace negotiations. After nine months without progress, an initial meeting had taken place in Abu Dhabi, with a follow-up round planned and European participation expected.

"We are also preparing for the possibility that the negotiations will not be successful and that, over the coming winter, we will have to continue supplying Ukraine with heating, electricity and all essential supplies, including water," he said.

"And we will continue to stand by Ukraine militarily."

He stressed that any peace agreement must include security guarantees to protect Ukraine against future Russian attacks.

In earlier comments during his trip to the South Caucasus, Wadephul said that Ukraine and Europe must be involved in any negotiations over the future of Ukraine.

Wadephul did, however, welcome the trilateral meeting between US President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen.

"Every conversation that takes place is a good conversation," he told DW during a visit to Azerbaijan on Wednesday.

Later on Thursday, Russian President Vladimir Putin said he had invited Europeans to Moscow for talks on the potential structure of future talks to end the war.

#563. Navigating grief in academia: ways to find balance

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Pamela Yeh is a professor of evolutionary biology at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Pamela Yeh with her mother in Los Angeles, California, in the late 1970s.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh

There are few things in this world that are more universal than grief. And yet, each person’s own particular grief can feel as unique as the person they are grieving for. I have been in academia for decades, but have heard little about grief in that time, so I wanted to share a few tips that helped me get through the early stages of grief when my mother died last year.

My mother grew up in deep poverty in Taiwan and she worked relentlessly throughout her life to give me and my siblings many opportunities. She was the first in her family to go to college, and at 23 years old, she moved to Canada to work as a nurse. After a few years of enduring Canadian winters, she had had enough and moved to sunny California. She met my dad there, and a few years later she gave birth to my sister, then me and then my brother. She raised us while working several jobs as a nurse. She cheered the three of us on throughout our lives. That’s not to say that she ever fully understood my career: she once described my work (I am an evolutionary biologist, specializing in birds and bacteria, at the University of California, Los Angeles) as “counting birds”.

She was adventurous, but between her family and work responsibilities, she didn’t have much time to travel. So, once she retired, I took her on fieldwork and conference trips with me whenever I could — to China, the Netherlands, Italy, Mexico, Japan and throughout the United States.

When her grandchildren came along, she helped them to learn how to read, to do maths and to speak Chinese. In the last years of her life, I had a small house built for her in our back garden in Los Angeles, so she would always be close to me. When you lose someone who is extremely close to you, your world is never the same.

When a loved one dies: how academia can support bereaved colleagues

When a loved one dies: how academia can support bereaved colleagues

In the weeks and months after she died, I found myself in a fog of shock and grief. I felt the need to be moving constantly: running, walking the dog, cleaning the house. At times, I could not be certain of my ability to conduct the high-level abstract and conceptual thinking that academia often requires, so I turned to Trevor Price, my former PhD adviser at the University of California, San Diego (who is now at the University of Chicago, Illinois). I explained my brain fog and deep grief, and he read over my work and made sure that I didn’t miss any crucial scientific arguments in some of the papers I was writing. Although I graduated more than two decades ago, he did not hesitate for one second to help me.

People won’t know that you need help until you reach out. And the earlier you do it, the more time and energy you can give yourself and the easier it will be for others to help.

Here are some tips that helped me to navigate the academic world while grieving.

Ideally, you should determine what support is available before it is needed. Institutions often have all sorts of resources and benefits for people experiencing grief. These might include time off for a bereavement, leave for family care, counselling and a break from teaching classes. I never knew, until my mother passed away, that I could have taken paid leave to take care of her while she was unwell: she had a debilitating stroke five months before she died. Make sure you understand (and ask questions) about your work contract and what your employer offers.

Sometimes, a family member’s illness can occur suddenly, and other times it might start off as one condition and snowball into something else. Talk to the chair of your department and to your colleagues as early as possible about getting cover for your courses and committees. Be creative and brainstorm which other people — including your colleagues, former advisers and former students and postdocs — might be able to step in and give your conference talks, guest lecture for your classes and conduct other activities that you might need help with.

Pamela Yeh (centre) with her parents, husband, son and dog on the front steps of her home in Los Angeles, California, in 2014.Credit: Courtesy of Pamela Yeh

I learnt this the hard way. I did not reach out to people early enough and was unrealistically optimistic about my mother’s health trajectory. While I waited for her to get better, I was so panicked about the thought of losing her that I became incapacitated. I couldn’t focus and, at times, I could barely do simple tasks such as answering e-mails, or making appointments for meetings. I told myself as soon as she was better, which would be any day now, I would catch up. And so, I didn’t have a realistic plan in place when she died.

You have to accept that you might not be at your best when it comes to research productivity, mentoring and teaching while you’re grieving. Ask someone to help with advising your students, and rely on colleagues or former students. You might have to reduce the frequency with which you meet your students, hold laboratory meetings and work with collaborators, and resort to advising through e-mail and video calls. And you might have to give less detailed comments on your students’ writing. I did all of the above during the first few weeks and months of grieving. I had an especially hard time giving advice to my graduate students who were doing field work. Ellie Diamant, a former PhD student of mine who is now a biologist at Bard College in Annandale-On-Hudson, New York, generously stepped in and met with many of my students. It took me a while to understand and accept that I simply wasn’t going to meet the normal standards I set for myself while going through this difficult time.

#562. 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck reveals an ingenious waterproofing trick

A 2,200-year-old Roman shipwreck off the coast of Croatia is revealing how ancient shipbuilders protected their vessels from the destructive forces of the sea. Researchers have discovered two distinct waterproofing recipes, including one that combined pine tar with beeswax. Even more remarkably, microscopic pollen grains preserved in the sticky coatings offer clues to where the ship was built and repaired during its lifetime.

For as long as humans have traveled by sea, shipbuilders have faced the challenge of keeping water out while protecting vessels from saltwater, microorganisms, and marine creatures such as shipworms. Despite their name, shipworms are actually marine mollusks that burrow into wood and can cause extensive structural damage.

Yet until the mid-20th century, archaeological studies of ancient vessels largely concentrated on their wooden components. The protective materials that made these ships seaworthy received comparatively little attention, and waterproofing substances remain an understudied aspect of ancient maritime technology.

In a new study published in Frontiers in Materials, researchers from France and Croatia investigated the protective coatings of Ilovik-Paržine 1, a ship dating to the Roman Republic that sank approximately 2,200 years ago off the coast of modern Croatia.

"In archaeology little attention is paid to organic waterproofing materials. Yet they are essential for navigation at sea or on rivers and are true witnesses of past naval technologies," said first author Dr. Armelle Charrié, an archaeometrist at the Laboratory of Mass Spectrometry of Interactions and Systems in Strasbourg. "Studying the coatings, we found two different kinds on this vessel: one made of pine tar, also called pitch, and the other of a mixture of pine tar and beeswax. Analysis of pollen in the coating made it possible to identify the plant taxa present in the immediate environment during the construction or repairs of the ship."

Since its discovery in 2016, the shipwreck and its cargo have been the subject of several scientific investigations. However, this is the first study to combine molecular analysis with the examination of ancient pollen to determine both the composition of the ship's waterproofing materials and the types of vegetation growing nearby when those coatings were produced or applied.

The research brought together specialists from the Department for Underwater Archaeology of the Croatian Conservation Institute and the 'ADRIBOATS' program of the Centre Camille Jullian at Aix-Marseille University in France.

"Some regions throughout the Adriatic have particular characteristics that led local populations to develop a specific shipbuilding style," said Charrié. "Only studies like ours offer an overview into these traditions which bear witness to genuine know-how and diverse traditions."

To uncover the ancient waterproofing recipes, the researchers examined the physical structure, molecular composition, and pollen content of the coatings. Among the techniques they employed was mass spectrometry, a powerful analytical method that allows scientists to identify substances and measure their abundance based on the masses of their molecular or atomic components.

An Ingenious Combination of Pine Tar and Beeswax

The team analyzed 10 samples of the ship's protective coating to determine the biological origins of the ingredients. Distinctive chemical signatures characteristic of pine trees appeared throughout the samples, revealing that the primary waterproofing material was pitch derived from heated conifer resin or tar.

Pitch is a thick, sticky substance that has been used for centuries to seal wooden vessels and protect them from water. When heated, it becomes easier to spread over surfaces and into gaps between wooden components.

One sample, however, contained evidence of a different recipe. Ancient shipbuilders had combined the pine tar with beeswax, creating a protective substance known to Greek shipbuilders as zopissa.

The addition of beeswax made the coating more flexible and easier to apply while hot. Flexibility would have been a valuable property aboard wooden ships, whose timbers could shift and flex as they encountered waves and changing environmental conditions.

Ancient Pollen Preserves a Record of the Ship's Past

The sticky nature of pitch gave it another remarkable property that ancient shipbuilders probably never considered. It could capture tiny airborne pollen grains from surrounding vegetation and preserve them for thousands of years.

Different plants produce pollen with distinctive shapes and structures, allowing scientists to identify the types of vegetation present in an area long after the plants themselves have disappeared. By examining both the variety and relative abundance of pollen grains embedded in the ship's coatings, the researchers narrowed down the possible locations where the pitch was manufactured or applied during repairs.

The pollen preserved aboard Ilovik-Paržine 1 pointed to a surprisingly diverse range of landscapes. Some of the plant species were characteristic of Mediterranean and Adriatic coastal areas and valleys, including forests dominated by holly oak and pine. Others were associated with matorral, a type of Mediterranean shrubland that can contain olive and hazel trees.

The discovery of alder and ash pollen suggested the presence of vegetation growing near rivers or coastlines, either close to the sea or farther inland. Smaller quantities of fir and beech pollen pointed to mountainous environments. Such vegetation is characteristic of the northeastern Adriatic coast, where the mountains of Istria and Dalmatia rise not far from the shoreline.

Evidence of Multiple Repairs Across the Mediterranean

The distribution and composition of the protective materials also revealed that the vessel likely received four or five distinct batches of waterproofing coatings.

The stern, or rear of the ship, and its central section shared the same coating. At the bow, or front of the vessel, researchers identified three batches that differed from one another. These variations suggest that the ship may have undergone a series of repairs using materials obtained from different locations around the Mediterranean.

Earlier investigations of the ship's ballast, the heavy material carried aboard a vessel to improve its stability, identified the ancient city of Brundisium as its likely place of construction. Known today as Brindisi, the port city lies on the southeastern coast of Italy and was an important maritime center in the ancient Roman world.

The new pollen evidence suggests that some of the waterproofing coatings were applied in the vicinity of Brundisium. Other layers may have been added along the northeastern Adriatic coast, near the region where the vessel ultimately sank.

The findings demonstrate how microscopic biological traces can reveal aspects of ancient maritime history that might otherwise remain hidden. Even when waterproofing materials appear chemically identical, the pollen trapped within them can preserve evidence of separate repair events and the environments in which they occurred.

"While it seems obvious that ships sailing long distances need repairs, it's simply not easy to demonstrate this," concluded Charrié. "Pollen has been very useful in identifying different coatings where the molecular profiles were identical."

Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Rocket Lab will add another satellite to a growing Japanese Earth-observation constellation today (Nov. 26), and you can watch the action live.

An Electron rocket carrying a radar imaging satellite for Tokyo-based Earth-observation company Synspective is scheduled to lift off from Rocket Lab's New Zealand launch site today, during a window that opens at 7:00 p.m. ET (0000 GMT and 1:00 p.m. on Nov. 27 in New Zealand).

You can watch the mission, called "Night Owls Never Sleep," via Rocket Lab starting about 30 minutes before liftoff. Space.com will carry the company's stream if, as expected, it's made available.

Synspective is building a network of "Strix" spacecraft equipped with synthetic aperture radar (SAR), which uses radio waves to generate detailed images of Earth's surface in both day and night lighting, as well as through cloud cover.

Today's launch will be Rocket Lab's 14th for Synspective to date, and there are a lot more coming. At the end of September, Rocket Lab announced a deal with the company for an additional 20 Electron missions between 2028 and 2031 — the largest commercial launch contract in the rocket's history. That agreement brought Synspective's total number of contracted Electron flights to 47.

Synspective aims to eventually establish a constellation capable of imaging locations anywhere on Earth at intervals of just a few hours.

If all goes to plan today, the Electron's kick stage will deploy the Strix satellite into low Earth orbit, 569 kilometers (353.6 miles) above our planet.

"Night Owl Never Sleeps" will be the 101st mission to date for Rocket Lab. Ninety-two of them have been orbital flights with Electron; the other nine have been missions with HASTE, a suborbital variant of Electron that allows customers to test sensors and other equipment in the hypersonic flight environment.

#560. EU Commission confirms it was targeted in cyberattack using AI tools

The European Commission was targeted by an "AI-generated cybercampaign," a spokesperson has said. This is the first time the bloc has publicly reported an AI-based cyberattack.

The European Commission confirmed on Thursday that it was ‌targeted by ⁠a ⁠cyberattack through the use of AI tools.

The incident was detected on October 22 and there was ‌no evidence ​of a data breach affecting Commission staff as a whole, European Commission spokesperson Thomas Regnier told reporters.

"This was an AI-generated ‌cybercampaign," he added.

Regnier did not elaborate on the attack or name a perpetrator. He said the Commission "has taken the necessary steps in response."

This is the first time the bloc reported an AI-assisted cyberattack.

Regnier's statement came after Politico reported earlier on Thursday that the Commission had been targeted. The report said the cyberattack disrupted several systems for 10 days and might have compromised large amounts of personal data. The European Commission has roughly 33,000 employees.

#559. Alexander Zverev faces fresh lawsuit from ex-girlfriend

World No. 1 tennis player Alexander Zverev is facing a new lawsuit related to a domestic abuse trial. The lawyer for his ex-girlfriend, Brenda Patea, told DW what the allegations are against the German player.

Alexander Zverev misrepresented the result of his 2024 domestic abuse trial, causing harm to his former partner and the mother of his child, Brenda Patea's lawyer has told DW.

The case ended without a verdict after both sides reached an out-of-court settlement. Zverev, who won the French and US Open in 2026, is alleged to have told French publication L'Equipe that: "I did everything I could, and my innocence has been proven."

As Zverev's lawyers noted in a statement sent to DW: "The criminal proceedings were discontinued... without any finding of guilt, and the presumption of innocence remains unaffected."

However, Zverev's statement has harmed Patea's standing and her career as an influencer, according to her lawyer, Michael Scheele.

"What she suffered after this interview in L'Equipe was published is nothing but a shitstorm. It's also detrimental to her business," Scheele told DW.

"We still don't know the truth objectively and we have an agreement in which he committed not to talk about the incident and the case at all," he added.

However, in the statement sent to DW, Zverev's lawyers asserted that "there has been no breach of any contractual obligations or violation of Ms. Patea’s personality rights."

Zverev had made similar comments before. On the day the settlement was reached, the tennis pro spoke to reporters at the 2024 French Open.

"That's what dropping the case is: That is innocence. They're not going to drop the case if you're guilty at the end of the day," he said.

The lawsuit, seen by DW, states that Zverev should be subject to "a fine of up to €250,000 ($275,000) to be determined for each instance of violation — and, in the event that such fine cannot be collected, substitute custodial detention of up to six months," should he be found guilty.

"Our client will defend himself against the lawsuit. If the statement attributed to him was indeed made in the form alleged, we consider it to be a permissible expression of opinion protected by Article 5(1) of the German Basic Law," they said.

"Our client would merely have expressed his personal conviction that he had done everything in his power to refute the allegations made against him and that he considers his innocence to have been confirmed by the outcome of the criminal proceedings. "He is fully entitled to hold and express this view."

The law firm, Schertz Bergmann, added that: "Unlike the opposing counsel, we intend to conduct these proceedings in court rather than in the press."

Scheele said he and his client did not want to go back to court but were frustrated in their efforts to resolve matters in other ways.

"We went forward writing to him in a polite way, asking him to sign and to declare that he's not going to repeat what he said. And he didn't reply. So we wrote twice more, no reply.

"That's when we had to decide to go to court, which was not the aim at the beginning. We wanted to avoid it, but we had no other choice."

Zverev, now resident in Monaco, is currently playing in the season-ending ATP Finals tournament in Turin.

#557. What is a thought made of? Why human consciousness may be beyond AI’s reach

The fundamental difference between human intelligence and artificial intelligence may have less to do with computing power than with the chemistry of memory. Researchers propose that the brain not only communicates through electrical signals but may also "write" and "read" memories through chemical interactions involving neurons, astrocytes, and the molecules surrounding them. By linking memory to emotion and thought, the theory raises an increasingly relevant question: Can computational power alone give rise to the kind of consciousness experienced by living organisms?

Hearing a familiar song can transport someone back decades. A distinctive scent can bring a forgotten person or place to mind, while recalling a terrifying experience can trigger both emotional and physical reactions within moments.

Like the human brain, computers can store and retrieve information. However, the mechanisms underlying biological memory may be fundamentally different.

A new review by Dr. Gerard Marx of MX Biotech Ltd. and Professor Chaim Gilon of the Department of Chemistry at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem explores the physical and chemical mechanisms that could link memory, emotion, and thought.

In their paper, "Consciousness, Memory and Intelligence: A Mechanistic Perspective," the researchers suggest that understanding memory requires more than studying neurons and their electrical activity. They argue that other brain cells, particularly astrocytes, and the intricate molecular environment surrounding them may also play essential roles.

Building on their previous research into the molecular foundations of memory, Marx and Gilon examine whether the processes responsible for storing and retrieving experiences could also shed light on the origins of intelligence, thought, and consciousness.

The Brain's Hidden Chemical Code for Memory

Central to the researchers' proposal is a model known as the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory.

According to this theory, memories emerge from interactions between three major components: brain cells, especially astrocytes working alongside neurons; the molecular substances surrounding those cells; and various chemicals, including metal ions, neurotransmitters, and gliotransmitters.

Rather than relying exclusively on electrical communication between neurons, the brain may use chemical processes to encode and retrieve information.

Astrocytes, which are abundant throughout the brain and maintain close interactions with neurons, are particularly important to this proposed mechanism. Marx and Gilon suggest that groups of astrocytes help process cognitive information through their interactions with neurons and the extracellular environment, the space and molecular material surrounding brain cells.

The new paper expands this hypothesis to explore the nature of thought itself. If the brain can physically encode an experience as a memory, the process of recovering that information, recognizing it, and interpreting its significance might contribute to the formation of thoughts.

One of the central arguments of the researchers' theory is that biological memories contain more than stored information. They are also closely connected to emotional experiences.

A scent associated with childhood may spark feelings of happiness. Hearing a familiar voice can provide reassurance, while remembering a frightening event may produce an immediate physical response.

Marx and Gilon contend that a physical model of memory must account for these emotional associations. Their proposed mechanism incorporates neurotransmitters and other chemical messengers that may help encode cognitive information alongside its emotional significance.

This potential biochemical connection between memory and emotion provides a starting point for investigating larger questions about how the brain generates thought, intelligence, and conscious experiences.

What Human Consciousness May Have That AI Lacks

The rapid development of artificial intelligence makes these ideas particularly relevant.

Although computers and brains can both retain and access information, the physical mechanisms behind these abilities may differ considerably. Computer memory is ultimately encoded in electronic hardware. Biological memory, the researchers propose, may instead depend on the intricate cellular and chemical machinery of living brain tissue.

This distinction becomes increasingly significant as AI systems grow more capable of performing tasks traditionally associated with human reasoning and intelligence.

Marx and Gilon challenge the assumption that simply increasing computational power and complexity will eventually produce consciousness comparable to that of a living brain. They argue that electronic systems lack the biological structures and emotional mechanisms found in living organisms.

The researchers are not suggesting that AI cannot develop increasingly advanced intellectual capabilities. Instead, they question whether demonstrating intelligent behavior is equivalent to possessing the biological mechanisms responsible for memory, emotion, and conscious experience.

Marx and Gilon emphasize that their theory does not solve the enduring mystery of consciousness. They explicitly acknowledge that the nature of conscious life remains poorly understood.

However, their proposed biochemical framework offers a different way to investigate the physical processes that may underlie mental activity. By examining interactions between brain cells and their chemical environment, the Tripartite Mechanism of Memory could provide researchers with another avenue for exploring how the mind works.

While their earlier research focused on how memories might be physically encoded within the brain, their latest work addresses a much broader problem.

Understanding how living brain tissue transforms experience into memory could eventually help explain how memories become thoughts, how conscious experiences arise, and what fundamentally distinguishes biological intelligence from artificial intelligence.

#556. Physicists trap antimatter in a breakthrough that could explain why the universe exists

Physicists at Northwestern University have achieved an unprecedented level of quantum control over a single positron, the antimatter counterpart of an electron. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists answer one of the most fundamental questions in physics: Why does the universe exist as we know it?

The researchers captured a rapidly moving positron produced through radioactive decay, slowed it down, and cooled it to a temperature just above absolute zero. They then confined the particle within a near-perfect vacuum, isolating it from ordinary matter, which would cause it to annihilate.

Using this approach, the team created what they call a "one-positron quantum cyclotron." Within this system, the positron behaves somewhat like an artificial atom, allowing researchers to observe and precisely manipulate its individual quantum energy levels.

The achievement lays the groundwork for what could become the most rigorous test yet of the fundamental symmetry between electrons and positrons. The Standard Model of particle physics predicts that the two particles should behave as nearly perfect mirror images of each other.

By measuring the positron's magnetic properties with unprecedented accuracy and comparing them with those of an electron, scientists could uncover previously undetected differences. Any unexpected discrepancy would point to a weakness in the Standard Model and potentially offer clues to why the universe contains so much more matter than antimatter.

The research was published in Physical Review Letters.

"Antimatter gets its popular charm from science fiction," said Northwestern's Gerald Gabrielse, who led the study. "If you take an electron and an anti-electron (or positron) and collide them together, they both disappear. We describe that as annihilation, a concept that fuels science fiction writers' imaginations. The big mystery of the universe is the Big Bang should have created equal amounts of matter and antimatter. But, if that were true, it would annihilate, and we'd be left with nothing. There's clearly something wrong with that theory, and that's what we're trying to figure out."

Gabrielse is the Board of Trustees Professor of Physics at Northwestern's Weinberg College of Arts and Sciences and director of the university's Center for Fundamental Physics. Thomas Myers, a Ph.D. student working in Gabrielse's laboratory, is the study's first author.

Searching for Cracks in the Standard Model

The Standard Model is one of the most successful theories in modern science. It describes the universe's fundamental particles and three of its four fundamental forces (electromagnetic, strong nuclear and weak nuclear forces). Countless experiments have verified its predictions with remarkable accuracy.

Despite those successes, the theory remains incomplete. One of its most significant shortcomings is its inability to explain the overwhelming abundance of matter compared with antimatter in the observable universe.

"We know the Standard Model has to be wrong somewhere -- or at least incomplete," Gabrielse said. "For example, it cannot predict why the universe exists, so that's a pretty big loophole. We're very precisely examining the most fundamental and simple systems to find where the theory breaks down. We hope to find an unambiguous answer."

Gabrielse has devoted decades of his scientific career to investigating this mystery. His research group previously developed methods for isolating individual electrons and determining their magnetic properties with exceptional precision.

He also helped establish the field of low-energy antimatter research by pioneering techniques for slowing, capturing, and cooling antiprotons. The latest achievement combines these two areas of expertise, extending the sophisticated quantum control previously demonstrated with electrons to an individual antimatter particle.

Almost everything on Earth is composed of three familiar particles: electrons, protons, and neutrons. A universe made of antimatter could contain their respective counterparts: positrons, antiprotons, and antineutrons. According to Gabrielse, if everything on Earth were constructed from antimatter instead of ordinary matter, distinguishing between the two would be remarkably difficult.

The dramatic differences emerge when matter and antimatter come into contact. An electron and a positron, for example, can annihilate when they encounter one another. This makes storing antimatter particularly challenging, as contact with the material walls of an ordinary container would almost certainly destroy the trapped particle.

"If we want to study antimatter, we must handle it carefully," Gabrielse said. "To be clear, it's not dangerous. We don't have enough antimatter to make an explosion."

To overcome this problem, the Northwestern researchers employed an advanced particle trap that uses carefully configured electric and magnetic fields. These fields keep the positron suspended in an empty region of space, preventing it from coming into contact with the surrounding material.

By effectively creating a container that does not require the particle to touch any physical walls, the team has managed to keep a single positron confined in Gabrielse's laboratory for months.

Capturing a positron presents another considerable technical hurdle. Certain atomic nuclei release positrons as they undergo radioactive decay. For their experiment, the researchers used sodium-22, a rare radioactive isotope of sodium. Positrons emitted during this process initially carry tremendous amounts of energy.

The physicists substantially reduced the particle's speed before directing it into the trap's near-perfect vacuum. Inside, the temperature is maintained at approximately 300 millikelvins, equivalent to just 0.3 degrees above absolute zero.

Under these extremely cold conditions, the positron can settle into its lowest possible quantum energy state.

"We cool it down so much that it's in its quantum ground state," Gabrielse said. "We actually coaxed this very fast positron to sit there and behave for months at a time."

Putting Matter and Antimatter to the Ultimate Test

Beyond capturing and cooling the positron, the researchers demonstrated that they could deliberately change its individual quantum energy states and detect those changes.

Using microwaves tuned to specific frequencies, the physicists transferred carefully controlled amounts of energy to the particle and observed the resulting transitions between quantum states. This ability is crucial to their larger objective of determining the positron's magnetic properties with exceptional accuracy and comparing them directly with those of an electron.

In earlier research, Gabrielse and his colleagues used a one-electron quantum cyclotron to determine the electron's magnetic moment, a measure of its magnetic properties, with a precision of approximately one part in 10 trillion. That achievement ranks among the most precise measurements ever performed on an elementary particle.

The team now intends to conduct an equivalent measurement using the trapped positron. Comparing the two results could provide an extraordinarily sensitive test of current particle physics theories and potentially uncover evidence of previously unknown physics.

"Current theories suggest that there will be no difference in the two measurements," Gabrielse said. "If it turns out they are not equal, that would be the biggest discovery in physics in the last century."

The study, "One-positron quantum cyclotron," received support from the National Science Foundation (grant number 2110565).

#555. Anthropic trading tests investors' appetite for AI

Anthropic was valued at $2 trillion after shares started trading on the Nasdaq following a record $81 billion IPO. Its performance will put investor confidence in AI to the test.

Shares of US artificial intelligence (AI) giant Anthropic saw their first day of trading on Thursday on the US tech-heavy Nasdaq stock exchange.

Anthropic is one of the global leaders in AI technology and is best known for its Claude chatbot.

The stock opened at $111.50 (€101.7) — that's 34% higher than the IPO price of $83 and puts the company's valuation at $2 trillion. Anthropic stock ended the first day of trading at $97 per share.

The company's share performance is being seen as a key test of investor appetite for AI, as stock prices have swung wildly in recent months.

The San Francisco-based company behind the Claude AI tool has offered 980 million shares at $83 per share, raising a record $81 billion.

This valued the firm at $1.5 trillion, well above market estimates of around $1.3 trillion.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Anthropic is the first big AI company to go public. Its main competitor, ChatGPT-maker OpenAI,  has reportedly pushed its IPO to 2027.

Issuing shares on the stock market is essentially a way to raise money and avoid taking on debt.

Anthropic has already taken on $6.2 billion in debt and is not yet making a profit. At the same time, it faces massive bills for computer power and data centers.

That specific financial situation is one of the reasons for persistent concern that the AI boom might be a bubble that will eventually burst.
